extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, patent examiners, and law students
extracted.subtask_description: Doctrinal guidance for determining whether a process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter, or design qualifies as an 'invention' (vs. skillful work or aggregation) under patent law; explains black‑letter rules, evidentiary presumptions, and important exceptions with case examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not invention when ordinary skill would produce it
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not invention to produce a process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter or design which any skillful mechanic, electrician, chemist, or other expert would produce whenever required to effectuate a given result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justice Bradley: patent laws are intended to reward those who make substantial discoveries and not to grant monopolies for every slight advance or 'trifling device' which would naturally occur to any skilled mechanic. Routine developments that any competent practitioner would devise are to be treated as mere skill, not invention. Numerous cases apply this rule; courts weigh whether claimed advance is above ordinary mechanical or engineering skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of invention can be proved by independent contemporaneous contrivance or reproduction from taught prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: The absence of invention may be established by evidence that a considerable number of persons, acting independently of each other, and without receiving information from the patentee, did in fact contrive the improvement claimed not long after he produced it; or by teaching a mechanic the prior art and proving that, without exercising any invention, he promptly produced the improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidentiary route to show lack of invention: contemporaneous independent invention by many persons or a demonstration that a skilled mechanic, given the prior art, could promptly make the improvement without inventive effort. By contrast, a skilled mechanic reconstructing an older thing after seeing the patented thing does not necessarily prove lack of invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: First attainment of a long-sought result indicates invention despite simplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: If a particular result was long desired and sometimes sought but never attained, want of invention cannot be predicated of a device or process which first reached that result merely because the means are simple or seem obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where prior attempts and failures show the result was long sought, the fact that the successful device uses simple means does not negate invention; solved problems often seem easy in hindsight to those who could not have solved them. The doctrine complements the rule that routine skill is not invention by requiring consideration of prior unsuccessful attempts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial success and prior failed attempts can support invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Where several improvements mutually contributed to introduce an unused invention into public favor, a presumption in favor of either of those improvements being an invention arises out of the commercial success of the invention thus improved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commercial success is a relevant secondary consideration supporting inventiveness, especially when prior attempts failed. However, if prior attempts failed due to unskillfulness or lack of familiarity with the prior art, those failures may not be material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excellence of workmanship alone is not invention
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not invention to produce an article which differs from some older thing only in excellence of workmanship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish planning/creating a new improvement (invention) from merely executing an existing plan with superior workmanship. Improving finish, execution, or making a commercially acceptable version of a previously planned device is not inventive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substituting superior materials is generally not invention (with exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not invention to substitute superior for inferior materials in making one or more or all of the parts of a machine or manufacture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts often treat substitution of materials as selection/adaptation (judgment and skill) rather than invention. Selecting a material from options recommended in prior art is not inventive. Important exceptions: substitution may be inventive if it (a) involves a new mode of construction, (b) develops new properties or uses, (c) produces a new mode of operation or new function, (d) yields the first practical success in the art, (e) increases efficiency or saves decisive cost of operation, or (f) if the superiority could not have been known beforehand and practice demonstrates unexpected advantages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scaling up (enlargement/strengthening) is not invention
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not invention to so enlarge and strengthen a machine that it will operate on larger materials than before.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merely producing a larger version of an old machine (copying on a larger scale) is treated as construction, not invention (e.g., circular saw adapted to sawing logs vs. prior smaller saws). Similar decisions have applied where a previously known design is duplicated at a larger scale without novel functional change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Change in degree or size alone is not invention
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not invention to change the size or degree of a thing, or of any feature or function of a machine or manufacture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: making sides of paving stones rougher, concentrating valve openings into a smaller space, increasing weight of a hand-wheel — courts have held these mere changes of degree not patentable. Whether a change in amount of an ingredient or degree of an agent (heat, etc.) is inventive depends on application of other rules and the functional consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative reduction or change that produces significant system-level effects can be invention (Edison exception)
rubrics_metrics.description: A reduction in size or a quantitative change that materially alters ratios or produces large, unforeseen system-level advantages may constitute invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by Edison incandescent light patent: reducing filament diameter from 1/32" to 1/64" materially multiplied resistance-to-radiating-surface ratio, enabling systemic changes (smaller conductors, different generators) and resulting economies. Cheapness, simplicity, ease of operation, and economical/efficient performance as compared with prior structures are indicators of invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggregation of old elements is not invention; combinations must produce a joint/cooperating new result
rubrics_metrics.description: Aggregation is not invention in processes, machines, or manufactures; a combination of old elements is patentable only if the constituents so enter into it that the combination produces a new and useful result as the product of the cooperative action of all elements, not merely the sum of separate results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mere assemblage of several old features that each continue to perform their former function (no joint operation producing a new result) is a mere aggregation and invalid. Case examples: self-feeding stoves combining prior features; pencil with rubber—no joint function. The combination must produce a result due to the elements acting together.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination elements need not act simultaneously — successive cooperative action can support patentability
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule does not require all parts of a patentable combination to act at the same time; successive action of elementary parts that contributes to a single practical result can form a valid combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justice Curtis: if arranged so successive action of each contributes to produce one practical result that is the product of the whole, a valid claim may be made. It is enough that, in normal progressive use, the parts co-operate some of the time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duplication of parts is not invention unless it creates a new mode or unitary result
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not invention to duplicate one or more parts of a machine or manufacture; duplication is patentable only if the duplication causes a new mode of operation or produces a new unitary result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Duplicating components without producing any new joint function or unity of operation is treated as mere mechanical expedient and not inventive.
